newsitem.title: UK: NWE naphtha down but 150kt Skikda supply heads eas.
newsitem.headline: NWE naphtha down but 150kt Skikda supply heads eas.

text.p: NWE naphtha prices ended lower on Thursday but traders said 150,000 tonnes of Mediterranean material was believed to have been fixed for the Far East, which should steady prices here.
"That's probably about right," one trader said, referring to the amount sailing east.

"If all this material is going then I think we will move from an oversupply situation to a balanced situation for Europe," he said, cautioning that he would wait to see exactly how much ended up going to the Far East.
"I would anticipate the crack spread to stabilise rather than be under pressure (if all that supply goes)."
March swaps, hit by lower crude prices and by what some traders said was sluggish end-user demand and adequate prompt supplies, fell $2 to $204/$205 a tonne.

NWE cargoes were notionally assessed at $206/$209 cif, steady to down about a $1 from Wednesday. No NWE cargo deals were heard done and an offer at $207 was quickly pulled when a buyer stepped in, sources said.
One trader said barges traded at $204 fob ARA and he believed the backwardation in the swaps had now flattened out, but this was not borne out by others' assessments.
He said that naphtha's fundamentals were bullish, with no unsold cargoes to be found, but that naphtha looked overvalued when compared to other products prices.

The Japan market is still tight and as long as the Far East continues to suck cargoes away from Europe, it will support prices here, he said. That means cargoes should be well supported near $200 cif after already falling from highs near $230 earlier this month.
"No one is sitting on a cargo without a home," he said. "All we need is for Brazil to step in and say naphtha is cheap, and the market will really go up."
Marc Rich fixed the 65,000 tonne Sibonina tanker from Skikda to Japan for loading March 3, according to shipping sources.
British Petroleum fixed the 50,000 tonne Alkyonis for loading out of Skikda on March 15 for Japan, the sources said.
A trader said there was another, smaller vessel fixed out of North Africa for Asia, bringing the total to 150,000 tonnes. This last fixture was not confirmed.
The shipping sources said Fleet, the shipping arm of J. Aron, fixed the 65,000 tonne Sitamona out of Rotterdam on March 3 destined for Japan, but it was not certain that this was for naphtha.
